findings.title: Raw recovery codes sent to user storage in plaintext
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes to JSON and passes them to the user storage provider through updateCredential. Local storage only keeps hashed codes, so this changes the security contract: every federated provider that accepts this credential type receives, and probably persists, cleartext recovery codes. Consider sending hashed codes instead, or documenting this behaviour explicitly.

findings.title: Federated recovery codes are never consumed or removed
findings.body: When the credential comes from federated storage, createFromCredentialModel rebuilds the model from the provider's data. Nothing marks the used code as consumed, so the same code stays valid and allCodesUsed() never becomes true. Separately, removeStoredCredentialById only touches local storage, so a federated credential would never be removed even if it were used up. The result is that codes stay reusable indefinitely and the user is never prompted to regenerate them.

findings.title: Federated credential data format may not match the expected model format
findings.body: getCredential returns whatever CredentialModel the federated provider exposes. The authenticator and the login bean then call RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel on it, which expects Keycloak's internal JSON format with hashed codes and numbers. A provider that stores raw data in the shape this PR's own updateCredential input implies (a JSON list of raw codes) will make parsing fail. It will also make getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get() throw, which surfaces as a 500 on the login page.

findings.title: getCredentials can throw NPE for unknown user
findings.body: getCredentials dereferences myUser without a null check. If the user is not in the map, accessing myUser.recoveryCodes throws a NullPointerException. Other methods in this class, such as isConfiguredFor and getDisableableCredentialTypesStream, guard against a null user.
